title: Seven Indian American Women Named to Forbes' 50 Over 50 List
excerpt: From the CEO of a $26 billion manufacturing company to the co-founder of Stop AAPI Hate, Indian American women are well represented on Forbes' annual list of entrepreneurs and changemakers over 50.
body:
• Seven Indian American women appear on the Forbes 50 Over 50 list of 200 entrepreneurs, investors, creators, and entertainers
  • Six are featured in the Entrepreneurs category, while Manjusha Kulkarni of Stop AAPI Hate is listed under Impact
  • The group includes CEOs of billion-dollar companies, venture founders, and pioneers in social advocacy
  • Jayshree Ullal of Arista Networks is among America's wealthiest female executives

Seven Indian American women have been named to the Forbes 50 Over 50 list, a curated selection of 200 entrepreneurs, investors, creators, and entertainers who have achieved notable success after the age of 50. Their presence across the Entrepreneurs and Impact categories reflects the growing breadth of Indian American women's influence in American business and public life.

Manjusha Kulkarni: Fighting Hate

The lone Indian American in the Impact category, Manjusha Kulkarni co-founded Stop AAPI Hate, which became America's leading aggregator of hate incidents against Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders during the Covid-19 pandemic. Kulkarni also serves as Executive Director of AAPI Equity Alliance, a coalition advocating for the rights of the Asian American community in Southern California. In 2014, she received the White House Champions of Change award for her work in improving healthcare access for South Asian Americans.

Six Leaders in Entrepreneurship

The remaining six women are all featured in the Entrepreneurs category, spanning industries from manufacturing to cybersecurity.

Revathi Advaithi leads Flex, a global manufacturing and supply-chain company with $26 billion in annual revenue and 200,000 employees. Since becoming CEO in 2019, she has steered the company through major supply chain disruptions while expanding its manufacturing footprint.

Jayshree Ullal has served as president and CEO of Arista Networks, a computer networking firm, since 2008. Born in London and raised in India, Ullal is one of America's wealthiest female executives. She owns approximately 5% of Arista's stock and also sits on the board of Snowflake, the cloud computing company.

"Increasingly it's not about knowing all the answers but asking the right questions and figuring out how to get the right answer."

— Padmasree Warrior, Founder-CEO of Fable

Padmasree Warrior has held CTO positions at both Cisco and Motorola and is currently the founder-CEO of Fable, a platform for social reading and book clubs that raised over $28 million. A Cornell-trained engineer, Warrior has been a vocal advocate for STEM education and its role in driving creativity.

Poornima DeBolle is the co-founder and chief product officer at Menlo Security, a cloud and network security company that raised $100 million in Series E funding at a valuation of $800 million.

Ann Mukherjee made history in 2019 as the first woman of color to become chair and CEO of Pernod Ricard North America, one of the world's largest wine and spirits companies. She launched Absolut's #SexResponsibly campaign, drawing on personal experience to raise awareness about the connection between responsible drinking and consent.

Anita Gupta is the founder and chief portfolio officer at KiwiTech, a company that helps early- to growth-stage startups build products, raise capital, and scale. Under her leadership, KiwiTech has invested in over 500 startups, focusing on disruptive innovation.

A Pattern of Growing Representation

The presence of seven Indian American women on the Forbes 50 Over 50 list adds to a growing pattern of recognition for the community. Indian Americans have become increasingly visible in leadership positions across corporate America, though representation among women has historically lagged behind their male counterparts.

The Forbes list recognizes that career achievements do not have an expiration date. Each of the seven women built or expanded their most significant ventures well past their 50th birthday, challenging conventional narratives about innovation being a young person's domain.

From advocating for hate crime victims to running a $26 billion manufacturing operation, the seven honorees represent the range of fields where Indian American women are making an impact — and the depth of experience they bring to each one.
